readme.title: What this module covers
readme.html:
What this module covers

This module explains how AWS charges for its services, through three pricing principles and three main cost drivers, and which tools help you estimate, track, budget and forecast spending. It then covers where help comes from, comparing the AWS Support plans and the extra resources around them, such as re:Post, solutions architects, AWS Professional Services, AWS Marketplace and the AWS Partner Network. A closing real-life example applies these ideas to cost optimization across EC2, RDS and S3.

readme.title: Lessons
readme.html:
Lessons

Module 11 Introduction

  1. Introduction to Pricing and Support: the two questions the module answers, told through the coffee shop's bills, broken espresso machine and waste.

AWS Pricing

  1. AWS Pricing Concepts: pay as you go, save when you commit, pay less by using more, and the compute, storage and outbound data transfer cost drivers.
  2. AWS Pricing and Billing Services: consolidated billing with AWS Organizations, and a side-by-side guide to the billing dashboard, AWS Budgets, AWS Cost Explorer and the AWS Pricing Calculator.

AWS Support

  1. AWS Support Plans: a comparison table of the five plans, TAMs, the 2027 end-of-support notice and help beyond the plans.
  2. AWS Marketplace and AWS Partners: the catalog of third-party software, data and services, and the AWS Partner Network with its partner benefits.

Cloud in Real Life

  1. Cost Optimization: rightsizing, Spot Instances, auto scaling, read replicas, S3 storage classes and VPC endpoints in one architecture.

readme.title: Key takeaways
readme.html:
Key takeaways

  • AWS pricing rests on three principles: pay as you go, save when you commit and pay less by using more.
  • Compute, storage and outbound data transfer are the three fundamental cost drivers, and inbound transfer is usually free.
  • AWS Organizations, not the billing dashboard, consolidates billing for many accounts into one bill sent to the primary account.
  • The billing dashboard shows current charges, AWS Budgets is the one tool that alerts on thresholds, AWS Cost Explorer analyzes and forecasts spending, and the AWS Pricing Calculator estimates costs before deployment.
  • Support plans are cumulative, from free Basic Support through Developer, Business and Enterprise On-Ramp to Enterprise, with faster responses and more personal help at each step.
  • The course notes that Developer, Business and Enterprise On-Ramp Support will be discontinued on January 1, 2027.
  • Only Enterprise On-Ramp and Enterprise include technical account managers, and Enterprise alone has a 15-minute response for critical outages.
  • AWS re:Post, the Trust and Safety Center, solutions architects, AWS Professional Services and AWS documentation add help outside the plans.
  • AWS Marketplace offers ready-made third-party software, data and services, and the AWS Partner Network helps partners build, market and sell AWS-based solutions.
  • Rightsizing, Spot Instances, auto scaling, read replicas, the right S3 storage class and VPC endpoints combine into significant savings.

readme.title: Summary
readme.html:
Summary

Paying for AWS comes down to three pricing principles, three cost drivers and a set of billing tools that each answer a different question: who pays, what is being spent, when to raise an alarm, what drives the bill, and what a new design will cost. Help scales with need, from free Basic Support to an Enterprise plan with a designated TAM, and reaches past the plans to community answers, AWS experts, consultants, Marketplace software and partners. The closing example shows that savings come from tuning a whole architecture rather than a single service. Module 12 moves on to migrating resources to the cloud.

aws-pricing-concepts.html:
AWS Pricing Concepts

Objectives

  • Explain the core ideas of AWS pricing.
  • Name the factors that drive cost.

Notes

Three pricing principles

  • Most services are pay-as-you-go: you pay for the services you pick, while you use them, with no lengthy contract or licensing.
  • Pay as you go: no upfront cost or commitment, so it suits variable or uncertain workloads and shifting needs without over- or underprovisioning.
  • : a usage commitment, usually 1 or 3 years, earns big discounts on steady workloads.
    • Example: price certain services, such as compute, below On-Demand.
  • : lower the unit price as usage grows, and some services use tiered pricing.
  • Committing and using more sound alike, but one rewards a time commitment, the other sheer volume.

Cost drivers

  • Price varies by service category, configuration, Region and pricing model, so check each pricing page.
  • The three main drivers are compute, storage and .
  • Compute (EC2, Lambda, ECS): processing power over time, per hour or second, from launch until you stop the instance, unless a reservation fixed the price.
  • Storage (S3, EBS): the amount provisioned or used and for how long, typically per gigabyte, across options for keeping, reaching, securing and analyzing data.
  • S3 tiers let cost follow how often and how fast you read data.
  • S3 has six cost components: storage, requests and retrieval, transfer and acceleration, management and analytics, replication, and Lambda processing.
  • Data transfer: inbound and most same-Region traffic is free, with exceptions, while outbound data is pooled across services and billed per gigabyte at falling rates.
  • Example: downloads from a static website hosted in S3 count as outbound transfer.
  • Exam guide update verified 2026-10-09, Understanding data transfer charges Incoming data transfer costs are nothing for data coming from the internet into AWS, while outgoing data transfer costs apply to data leaving for the internet or for another Region.

Worked example: a nonprofit on EC2

  • Compute: of 500+ instance types with different CPU and memory, the donation app uses t4g.nano, the cheapest that fits.
  • Storage: its cost follows the configured capacity.
  • Data transfer: sending data out for analytics is outbound, priced by volume and by the destination Region or internet source.

Visuals

  • Pricing flashcards: one card per principle, showing its benefit.
  • Cost driver accordion: one panel each for compute, storage and data transfer.
  • Pricing scenario graphic: three markers tracing each driver through the nonprofit's instance.

Key takeaways

  • The principles: pay as you go, save when you commit, pay less by using more.
  • Committing earns a time discount, while using more earns a volume discount.
  • The fundamental drivers are compute, storage and outbound data transfer.
  • Inbound transfer is usually free, and outbound is billed per gigabyte.

Scenarios

  • Visitors downloading from an S3 static website: outbound transfer charges.
  • A nonprofit's donation app: , EBS capacity and outbound data shape its bill.

Terms

  • Pay as you go: Paying only for what you use, with nothing upfront.
  • Save when you commit: Discounts for a usage commitment, usually 1 or 3 years.
  • Pay less by using more: Volume and tiered discounts as usage grows.
  • Savings Plans: 1-year or 3-year plans priced below On-Demand for certain services.
  • Cost drivers: Compute, storage and outbound data transfer.
  • Outbound data transfer: Data leaving AWS, billed per gigabyte.
  • Amazon S3 Object Lambda: An S3 data processing feature with its own charge.

AWS Pricing and Billing Services

Objectives

  • Explain what , the billing dashboard, and are for.
  • Explain what the is for.

Notes

Single or consolidated billing

  • A standalone account gets its own monthly bill.
  • With , subaccounts (by team, project, department or any split) link to a primary account that alone receives the bill and sees all spend.
  • AWS Organizations sets this up, adding central management, discounts and stronger security.

Telling the tools apart

Tool Gives you Use it for
AWS Organizations Creating, grouping and governing accounts, account-level security policies, one payment method One bill and shared policies across accounts
Billing and Cost Management dashboard Monthly forecast, top services by cost, charges, usage, reports, invoices, payment methods A first look at spend, or paying
AWS Budgets Custom budgets by service, cost category or tag, including and Reserved Instance utilization or coverage Warnings near or past a limit
AWS Cost Explorer Charts of cost and usage over time by service, linked account or tag, with trends and Reserved Instance advice Seeing what drives spend
AWS Pricing Calculator An itemized estimate from the instance types, storage and transfer volumes you enter Pricing or comparing designs before deploying
  • AWS Billing Dashboard (the video) and (the course text) name the same tool.
  • The dashboard links to budget and consolidated billing features, but AWS Organizations groups the accounts.
  • Budgets and Cost Explorer both forecast, but only Budgets sends threshold alerts.

Tags

  • are resource metadata that let one search find related resources, such as all development ones.
  • Cost Explorer can allocate costs by tags such as project, department or environment, showing who drives spend.
  • Exam guide update verified 2026-10-09, AWS cost allocation tags AWS cost allocation tags come in two types, AWS-generated and user-defined, and you must activate each before it appears in Cost Explorer or on a cost allocation report.
  • Exam guide update verified 2026-10-09, What are AWS Cost and Usage Reports? The AWS Cost and Usage Report holds the most detailed AWS cost and usage data, broken down by hour, day or month and by your tags, delivered as files to an bucket you own.

Key takeaways

  • AWS Organizations, not the billing dashboard, consolidates billing.
  • The dashboard is the first stop for charges and payments.
  • Only AWS Budgets alerts on thresholds.
  • Cost Explorer analyzes and forecasts spend, including by tag.
  • The Pricing Calculator estimates costs before deployment.

Scenarios

  • A monthly cost limit needing notifications: AWS Budgets.
  • Finding which project drives cost: tag-based allocation in Cost Explorer.

Terms

  • Consolidated billing: One bill for linked accounts, sent to the primary account.
  • AWS Organizations: Central multi-account management and billing.
  • AWS Billing and Cost Management dashboard: The central billing view.
  • AWS Budgets: Custom budgets with threshold alerts.
  • AWS Cost Explorer: Cost and usage analysis and forecasts.
  • Tags: Metadata labels that group resources.
  • Tag-based cost allocation: Grouping costs by tag.
  • AWS Pricing Calculator: A web tool for cost estimates.

Marketplace basics

  • A curated catalog of thousands of listings, mostly from independent software vendors (ISVs).
  • It spans discovery, trial, purchase, deployment and management, with pricing and reviews per listing.

Why use it

  • Reusing existing software cuts total cost of ownership and speeds innovation.
  • Buying is simpler, deploying and scaling are quick, and charges join your AWS bill.
  • Pricing can be free, pay-as-you-go or annual.
  • Compliance-ready software is quicker than an in-house build or working from documentation.

What you can buy

  • Software for security, networking, storage, ML and more, plus data and services.
  • : business (project management), marketing (customer engagement) and collaboration (file sharing) apps.
  • ML and AI: prebuilt models (image recognition, ) and training algorithms.
  • Data and analytics: datasets, BI and data integration tools.
  • Industry views, like healthcare tools for patient records or risk prediction.

AWS Partner Network

  • A global community of tech and consulting firms building customer solutions with AWS, solving problems and adding value.
  • Customers can hire partners, like a retailer adding ML personalization.
  • Partner benefits:
    • Funding, via partner programs, to build, market and sell with AWS.
    • Events (webinars, workshops, in person) for networking, updates and AWS experts.
    • Partner-centered content within the wider AWS Training and Certification, from certification to one service or goal.

cost-optimization.html:
Cost Optimization

Objectives

  • Describe techniques.

Notes

Look across services

  • Solutions usually combine services, so look for savings across the design (here EC2, RDS in a VPC, and S3).
  • EC2 is where many teams look first.

Amazon EC2

  • : measure real workload needs and resize to fit.
  • , a cost-minded sidekick, flags overprovisioned instances.
  • sell spare EC2 capacity at up to 90 percent off On-Demand, for flexible, interruption-tolerant jobs.
  • Some firms halved compute costs with Spot for noncritical work.

Auto scaling and cleanup

  • Auto scaling replaces hand-managing a fleet and sheds surplus capacity as demand falls.
  • Application load balancing spreads traffic across instances.
  • Forgotten EBS volumes and snapshots keep billing until deleted.

Amazon RDS

  • Rightsize databases too; storage autoscaling matches storage to demand.
  • Read replicas scale reads horizontally, sparing the primary a bigger, costlier instance.
  • Caching hot data in also lightens the primary.

Amazon S3

  • suits unknown or shifting access, and suits data read once or twice a year.
  • Compress text-heavy objects, for instance with a on upload.
  • Lifecycle policies can delete old versions; one customer paid for 10 years of daily backups but needed 30 days.

Data transfer

  • Transfer is not always free, so keep cross-AZ and internet traffic low; as with road traffic, less is better.
  • This squares with AWS Pricing Concepts: in-Region transfer is usually, not always, free.
  • VPC endpoints connect a VPC privately to supported services, and one used for S3 trims transfer costs, notably out-of-Region.

The bigger picture

  • Small tweaks add up and often improve performance and reliability too.
  • Aim for the right balance of cost, performance and operational efficiency.

Visuals

  • Architecture diagram: four markers (EC2, auto scaling, RDS, S3) placing each technique.

Key takeaways

  • Rightsize EC2 with AWS Compute Optimizer, and RDS with storage autoscaling.
  • Spot Instances cut up to 90 percent for interruption-tolerant work.
  • Auto scaling trims idle capacity, and deleting unused EBS volumes and snapshots stops waste.
  • Read replicas and ElastiCache spare the primary database from .
  • Match S3 classes to access, compress and expire old versions.
  • Keep cross-AZ and internet traffic low, and use VPC endpoints for S3.

Scenarios

  • Overprovisioned instances: AWS Compute Optimizer.
  • Years of unneeded backups: policies.

Terms

  • Rightsizing: Matching resources to real workload needs.
  • AWS Compute Optimizer: A service that flags overprovisioned compute.
  • Spot Instances: Discounted spare EC2 capacity for interruptible work.
  • AWS Auto Scaling: Automatic fleet sizing that drops spare capacity as demand falls; Module 2 covers scaling out.
  • RDS storage autoscaling: Resizes RDS storage with demand.
  • Read replica: An RDS copy that serves reads.
  • Amazon ElastiCache: A cache that offloads frequent reads.
  • S3 Intelligent-Tiering: A class for unknown or changing access patterns.
  • S3 Glacier Deep Archive: A low-cost class for data read once or twice a year.
  • Lifecycle policy: An S3 rule that can delete old object versions; Module 6 covers more.
  • VPC endpoint: A private VPC link to AWS services, off the public internet.
